archetype: Mono-black sacrifice-attrition engine that draws first and drains second — a control deck whose commander is a mana-free repeatable draw engine, whose kill is modular rather than singular (42 contained combo lines, 11 of them two-card infinites, sharing one pool of sac outlets, fodder and drains), and whose measured median game is the engine grinding a seat down while the ceiling lines wait for a piece the five-tutor suite can fetch.

role_assignment.default_role: CONTROL — you own the long game and should play like it. strategy:whos-the-beatdown's operational test is 'who has inevitability? — whoever loses the long game must be the beatdown', and nothing in a fair pod out-grinds a commander whose ability reads 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card' (cards.json oracle text) — no mana, instant speed, every spare body a card. strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock names the shape exactly: 'four-player games trend long, so inevitability compounds — engines are the default winning plan', and strategy:card-advantage's Commander correction calls 'engines that out-draw three players' the format's defining advantage. The goldfish sheet is a control deck's opening in every column at its own turn-10 horizon (goldfish_metrics.json, 10,000 iterations, seed 42), and the horizon is the right one: strategy:deckbuilding.curve puts the format at 'Commander games average 7–10 turns'. Unassisted / tutor-assisted by turn 10: renewable fodder 73.6% / 90.3%, a free sac outlet 73.8% / 90.0%, an ignition source 73.0% / 90.2%, a drain 66.9% / 87.7%, engine mana 60.6% / 85.0%. The commander lands on turn 4 in 7,249 of 10,000 games, mean 4.283, 91.7% by turn 6. Read the pair every time: the unassisted figure excludes tutors, rituals and cost reducers, the assisted one models a drawn, affordable tutor filling one missing half. Role is seat-relative (strategy:whos-the-beatdown, Commander correction): control against fair midrange, beatdown against anything that closes before turn seven.
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: The LOWEST life total at the table, measured against the drain rate the board you actually hold produces — and that rate is verified to differ by nearly a factor of two depending on which payoff is out. With Yawgmoth + Nest of Scarabs + a death-metering drain the engine produces SEVEN drains, 7 per opponent, 28 across the four-opponent pod, and 7 is proven a ceiling (stacks 002 and 003, checker.verdict == pass). With Mirkwood Bats on the like-for-like board it produces THIRTEEN, 13 per opponent, 52 across the pod, with 13 proven a ceiling five separate ways (stack 008, pass). Two accelerants are measured rather than argued: a counter-sink whose toughness exceeds 1 extends the bound — South Wind Avatar's 4 toughness is worth exactly +4 activations (stack 005, pass) — and stack 008's final checker solved the Bats line varying only the toughness of Bats itself, yielding 8 / 10 / 13 / 15 triggers at 0/1/2/3 counter slots. So the go decision is body arithmetic done before the first activation, which is the exact form strategy:critical-mass.storm-math prescribes: 'the go decision is arithmetic done *before* the first spell: the chain you can bank on versus the storm count, bodies, or damage the payoff needs for lethal. Count only hand and board; expected draws are a bonus, not a plan.' Trigger: go when (drains your board will produce) >= (the lowest opposing life total). One assembly is a seat, not a table — strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window's bar is met anyway, because 'Prefer win attempts that leave a rebuilt position if they fail' is free here: the failure state of this engine is a fistful of cards.

engines.engine: THE ENGINE, and it is a draw engine before it is a kill. The activated ability costs no mana — the price is 1 life and a body — so it runs at instant speed, on any turn, under any tax, and converts every spare creature into a card. Five checker-passed stacks record the draw explicitly; stack 005 runs 8 completed activations and ends with 8 cards drawn, library 52, you at 39 (40 start, −1 per activation ×8, +1 per lifegain event ×7). Protection from Humans is load-bearing in both directions: it makes Yawgmoth untargetable by his own ability, which is what BOUNDS every engine stack in this deck, and it blanks a slice of the format's creature removal.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); verified stacks 002/003/004/005/008 (all checker.verdict == pass) for activation counts, draws and life ledgers; goldfish_metrics.json commander mean_cast_turn 4.283, median 4, 7,249 of 10,000 on turn four, 91.7% by turn 6

engines.engine: The counter-to-body converter and the deck's structural hub: 'Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create that many 1/1 black Insect creature tokens.' It returns one body for the counter each activation spends — one only, and only after the death, so the loop is body-NEUTRAL while the counter lands on something that survives it and body-NEGATIVE otherwise. Stack 004 states the arithmetic flatly: killing one of your own creatures makes the activation minus one body — two creatures leave, Nest returns one. Stack 006 (pass) widens the trigger surface: a creature that ENTERS with a -1/-1 counter DOES trigger the Nest via CR 122.6/122.6a, and a counter placed on a creature already on the battlefield triggers it too, via CR 608.2c naming you as the actor. That makes Persist a Nest trigger as well as a reanimation. One precision worth carrying into print: Skullclamp's '+1/-1' is a static modification, not a counter, so equipping never triggers the Nest.
engines.evidence: oracle text; verified stacks 002/003/004/005 (bound and body arithmetic) and 006 (CR 122.6 entering-counters ruling); deck-facts synergy block reports Nest of Scarabs has NO entry in synergy_graph.json at all — the retrieval graph is blind to this deck's hub

engines.engine: The creation-side payoff, and the single most consequential measured fact on this deck. 'Whenever you create or sacrifice a token, each opponent loses 1 life' — a Yawgmoth activation paid with an Insect token supplies BOTH halves: the sacrifice is an activation cost paid after the ability is already on the stack (CR 602.2a, 602.2b routing to 601.2h), so the sacrifice trigger goes on the stack ABOVE the ability and resolves first, while the creation does not arrive until the Nest trigger resolves two resolutions later. Verified output on the board that stacks 002/003 measured at 7 drains: THIRTEEN triggers, 13 per opponent, 52 across the four-opponent pod (stack 008, pass). The same card is a LIABILITY on the Blowfly line: stack 007 (pass) proves Mirkwood Bats there triggers exactly twice, 2 life per opponent — worse than a death-metering drain by one — and HALTS the loop outright, because Bats' 2/3 body survives the forced -1/-1 counter, nothing dies, and Blowfly never re-triggers. Same card, same body, opposite verdicts: surviving the forced counter is fatal to a loop that needs something to die, and free value on a line that sacrifices deliberately.
engines.evidence: verified stack 008 (13 triggers / 52 pod; the final checker solved 8/10/13/15 triggers at 0/1/2/3 counter slots) and verified stack 007 (2 triggers, loop halts) — both checker.verdict == pass; oracle text

engines.engine: The second creation-side payoff, and the answer to the structural asymmetry that Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar all share — those four meter DEATHS, and a loop whose tokens die to their own counters starves them. Ayara reads 'Whenever Ayara or another black creature you control enters, each opponent loses 1 life and you gain 1 life', and Nest of Scarabs makes 1/1 BLACK Insect tokens, so Ayara is paid on the creation half. Her second ability — '{T}, Sacrifice another black creature: Draw a card' — is also a free sac outlet that draws, a second Yawgmoth for one body per turn. What is NOT established is the exact per-activation rate against stack 008's verified 13 and stack 003's verified 7. On oracle reading Ayara collects the creation half only (one per Nest token) where Bats collects creation plus sacrifice; that comparison is a candidate line, not a fact.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json) for both abilities and for the tokens' colour; card_roles.json assigns wincon:drain, sac-cost, utility:activated, threat:body; the per-activation rate is NOT verified — see candidate_missing_lines

engines.engine: Renewable fodder priced at {B}, with a condition the deck pays for itself: 'You may cast this card from your graveyard as long as you control a Zombie.' The Zombie shell is real — Warren Soultrader, Gray Merchant of Asphodel and Mikaeus, the Unhallowed are Zombies, Grave Titan makes 2/2 black Zombie tokens, and Nim Deathmantle makes its equipped creature a black Zombie. Every recast is a body for a sac outlet and, with a creation-side payoff out, a drain trigger. It is also half of the deck's most redundant unverified kill family: combo_details records Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler with each of Blood Artist, Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance and Ayara — four variants of one loop.
engines.evidence: oracle text; deck-facts combos block — Gravecrawler + Phyrexian Altar (two-card infinite, popularity 60,592) and four Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler + drain lines (popularity 32,914 / 29,620 / 19,747 / 17,211), all fully contained in the 99; none verified

engines.engine: The unconditional floor of the renewable-fodder class: '{1}{B}: Return this card from your graveyard to the battlefield tapped', forever, with no board condition to satisfy. Where Gravecrawler needs a Zombie, the Skeleton needs only mana — which is why it also anchors a contained infinite-mana line with Pitiless Plunderer and either Altar. It converts surplus mana into engine fuel on the exact axis strategy:critical-mass.storm-math cares about: the chain you can bank on, counted from board and hand.
engines.evidence: oracle text; deck-facts combos — Pitiless Plunderer + Ashnod's Altar + Reassembling Skeleton (infinite, popularity 52,227) and the Phyrexian Altar variant (33,056), both contained; unverified

engines.engine: A free repeatable sac outlet that also solves engine mana: 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Create a Treasure token.' Three jobs in one slot — outlet, treasure ramp, and a Zombie body that turns Gravecrawler on. Its life cost is the same currency Yawgmoth spends, which matters: with any drain that gains you 1 per trigger, the loop reads life-neutral rather than life-negative (strategy:life-as-resource — 'your life total is currency, not a score').
engines.evidence: oracle text; card_roles.json assigns ramp:dork, ramp:treasure, sac-cost, sac-outlet, threat:body, utility:activated — six roles in one card; mana_analysis.json lists it among the ten nonland B producers

engines.engine: Death-to-mana: 'Whenever another creature you control dies, create a Treasure token.' Every sacrifice the engine makes pays part of the next one, which is what turns a bounded chain into a longer bounded chain. It is one of five cards the goldfish sheet counts as ENGINE MANA (60.6% unassisted / 85.0% assisted by turn 10) and it appears in five contained infinite lines.
engines.evidence: oracle text; goldfish_metrics.json 'ENGINE MANA drawn' target, any_of = Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer, Phyrexian Tower, Black Market Connections, Warren Soultrader; deck-facts combos lists five contained lines containing it

engines.engine: The asymmetry converter, and the reason this engine is not merely a life-drain. 'Whenever a creature you control dies, each other player sacrifices a creature of their choice' — every activation the engine makes taxes three or four opponents at once. strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry is explicit that this is the shape that scales: 'Winning consistently means preferring asymmetric board wipes, repeatable value engines that out-scale three players, and effects that tax or drain every opponent at once.' A chain the drain ledger scores at 7 opposing life is simultaneously seven edicts per seat — the drain is the visible half of the clock, the board control is the half that decides fair games.
engines.evidence: oracle text; card_roles.json role removal:edict; the activation counts it multiplies are the verified ones from stacks 002/003/005/008

engines.engine: The second draw engine, and the one that works without the commander. '+1/-1' kills a 1/1 Insect, Faerie, Pest or Zombie token on equip and draws two — one mana, repeatable, and the deck makes 1/1s from Nest of Scarabs, Bitterblossom, Sedgemoor Witch and Black Market Connections. It is also the cleanest hedge against the recast tax: when Yawgmoth is answered the deck still draws (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance — 'A value commander can eat removal and re-buy — one recast of a cheap commander is a fine rate').
engines.evidence: oracle text; card_roles.json draw:burst + draw:engine; deck-facts roles histogram threat:tokens 7

engines.engine: A one-shot each-opponent drain sized by devotion, in a deck whose pip load is 75 black pips across 54 cards with a max of 3 (deck-facts mana block) — about as much devotion as a mono-black shell gets. It is also a Zombie, so it switches Gravecrawler on, and a recursion target for Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead, Phyrexian Reclamation and Nim Deathmantle. strategy:life-as-resource.philosophy-of-fire's Commander correction is the frame: against ~120 combined life 'reach must scale (each-opponent drains, commander damage, damage doublers) or be held as targeted finishing rather than the plan'.
engines.evidence: oracle text; deck-facts mana.pip_requirements B total_pips 75.0 across 54 cards, max_pips 3; card_roles.json recursion count 5 (Agadeem's Awakening, Persist, Phyrexian Reclamation, Reassembling Skeleton, Victimize)

engines.engine: The instant-speed answer to the sweeper, and the deck's one card that turns a wrath into cards rather than a rebuild. Sacrificing N creatures in response copies the spell N times, drawing N+1 and losing N+1 life. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math's Commander correction — 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package' — is answered here by converting the wave instead of holding it. Note the taxonomy has no ROLE pattern for this card at all (deck-facts names it, with Supernatural Stamina, in roles.no_role); absence of a role is not absence of the function.
engines.evidence: oracle text; deck-facts roles.no_role = [Plumb the Forbidden, Supernatural Stamina]; deck-facts note — 'Absence of a role is not absence of the function — the taxonomy simply has no pattern for them.'

engines.engine: A sweeper that is also an ignition source, which is why the deck can run four wipes without wiping itself. 'Put X -1/-1 counters on each creature' is you putting counters on creatures, and stack 006 (pass) settled that case explicitly — counters placed on a creature already on the battlefield trigger the Nest via CR 608.2c naming you as the actor. So the wipe that answers a board is simultaneously a Nest trigger and, with a creation-side payoff out, a drain. What is NOT settled is the token COUNT from one multi-creature, multi-counter event; stack 008 raised CR 603.2c for plural occurrences but on a line that places exactly one counter.
engines.evidence: oracle text; verified stack 006 (CR 608.2c ruling for counters placed on a creature already on the battlefield); verified stack 008 (CR 603.2c plural-event reasoning on a single-counter line); the token count is unverified — see candidate_missing_lines

engines.piece: The tutor suite (Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Beseech the Mirror, Diabolic Intent, Insatiable Avarice)
engines.engine: Five unrestricted tutors, and the goldfish sheet measures exactly what they buy: a tutor is drawn in 60.8% of games by turn 10, and every one of the four named kills multiplies roughly tenfold on the assisted line — Blowfly + Nest 2.6% → 32.1%, the Mikaeus package 1.7% → 26.2%, Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar 2.9% → 32.5%, Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler + a drain 1.1% → 20.0%. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors prices this precisely: a tutor is 'essentially an additional copy of any card in our deck' (Commander Mechanic), so 'k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of *every* card', against Lowry's cost — 'the more tutors you play, the less actual cards you get to play'. Diabolic Intent's sacrifice cost is not a cost in this deck; it is a trigger.
engines.evidence: goldfish_metrics.json target 'A tutor drawn' assembled_rate 0.608, mean_turn 3.092; each kill target's assembled_rate vs assembled_rate_assisted; bracket_report.json tutors list (5) and its note that tutor density 'is reported, never scored'

candidate_missing_lines.title: The Mikaeus family: does undying actually loop without a -1/-1 counter source, and does the bracket floor survive the answer?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The highest-stakes open question on the deck, because half the bracket floor rests on it. bracket_report.json lists 11 two-card infinites and SEVEN are Mikaeus plus a free sac outlet; the two_card_infinite driver is what forces bracket 4 ('11 two-card infinite(s); 11 assemble at mana value <= 6'). Mikaeus grants 'Other non-Human creatures you control get +1/+1 and have undying', and undying returns a creature 'if it had no +1/+1 counters on it, with a +1/+1 counter on it' — so on a plain reading the SECOND sacrifice of the same body finds a +1/+1 counter already there and does not return it. That would make Mikaeus plus an outlet a two-iteration line rather than an infinite one, unless something removes the +1/+1 counter each cycle. This deck has exactly that something and it is the commander: a -1/-1 counter from Yawgmoth annihilates the +1/+1 counter, which is presumably why combo_details ALSO records Mikaeus + Yawgmoth + Gray Merchant of Asphodel and Yawgmoth + Mikaeus + Ayara as separate lines. If the two-card readings do not hold on this board, seven of eleven infinites are really three-card lines routing through the commander, and the bracket conversation changes shape even if the computed floor does not (bracket_report.json's own note: 'Brackets are a conversation, not a calculator'). Nothing here is asserted — deck-facts states the rule: 'None is verified: a line is fact only once a stack artifact carries checker.verdict == pass.'

candidate_missing_lines.title: Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler + a drain: a measured, contained, wholly unresolved kill
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details records this loop four times, once per drain, at popularities 32,914 / 29,620 / 19,747 / 17,211, all fully contained. The mechanism is legible from oracle text alone: Soultrader ('Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Create a Treasure token') is itself a Zombie, so Gravecrawler stays castable from the graveyard, and the Treasure pays the {B} to recast it. Each cycle costs 1 life and gains 1 back from any of the four drains, so it reads life-neutral — the property that would make it unbounded rather than a forty-iteration chain. Three things a scenario must settle rather than assume: whether the life ledger is genuinely neutral once each drain's trigger order is written out; whether Ayara pays on Gravecrawler's re-ENTRY (creation side) while the other three pay on its death, and whether that changes the count; and what actually ends the loop, since the pilot must be able to stop at lethal. The urgency is that the deck is already counting on it: goldfish_metrics.json measures this family at 1.1% unassisted / 20.0% tutor-assisted by turn 10 (mean turn 6.514), the fourth named kill on the sheet — a rate the deck is credited with while not one of the four variants has been resolved.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar: the highest-bracket line present, and the only one nobody has resolved
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: bracket_report.json names this pair as the combo_content driver — 'highest-bracket line present: Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar', the only contained line tagged bracket 3 where the other 41 are tagged 1 — and goldfish_metrics.json already models its assembly (2.9% unassisted, 32.5% tutor-assisted by turn 10, mean turn 5.546). The oracle texts interlock: the Avatar's 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' feeds Exquisite Blood's 'Whenever an opponent loses life, you gain that much life', which feeds the Avatar again. What a scenario must establish and cannot assume: how many Exquisite Blood triggers one Avatar drain generates in a four-opponent pod (one per opponent, or one aggregate), whether the loop is mandatory and therefore terminates only when opponents' life hits zero under state-based actions, and how it interacts with CR 119.9 — stack 005 (pass) already found that gaining 0 life is not a life gain event on this deck's other Avatar line, which is exactly the kind of zero-magnitude edge that decides whether a lifegain loop starts at all. The deck's only verified Avatar result is stack 005's +4 activations and the refutation of Spellbook's 'Near-infinite' tag; that result does not transfer.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Ayara, First of Locthwain on the Yawgmoth line: what is the creation-only rate against Bats' verified 13 and a death-drain's verified 7?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Stack 008 (pass) proved a creation-side payoff collects TWO triggers per Yawgmoth activation because the sacrifice is an activation cost and the Nest token is a later creation; stack 003 (pass) proved a death-metering drain collects seven on the same shape of board because it is itself a body that must eventually die. Ayara sits in a third position neither stack measured: she pays on 'another black creature you control enters' — the Nest Insects are black — so she collects the CREATION half only, one per activation, and unlike Bats her death is not required to bank the last trigger. On oracle reading that puts her between the two verified rates, but 'between' is not a number, and the reason stack 008's answer was surprising is precisely that the naive count was wrong. The scenario should reuse the 002/003/008 board verbatim so the figure is comparable, and must also settle her second ability — '{T}, Sacrifice another black creature: Draw a card' — a once-per-turn free outlet that draws and may extend the bound the way South Wind Avatar's toughness did in stack 005.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Black Sun's Zenith + Nest of Scarabs: how many Insects does one sweeper make, and who is left holding them?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Stack 006 (pass) settled the qualitative half — counters you place on a creature already on the battlefield trigger the Nest via CR 608.2c — so a sweeper reading 'Put X -1/-1 counters on each creature' is also a Nest ignition. The quantitative half is open, and it is the whole value of the card: Nest says 'create that many' per event, and stack 008 (pass) raised CR 603.2c for plural occurrences within one event but only on a line placing exactly one counter. The open questions: whether each affected creature is a separate 'put' event, whether X counters on one creature yields X Insects, and what the board looks like afterwards — the wipe kills your own 1/1s, but the Insects it creates arrive as a state-based-action-checked wave. With Mirkwood Bats surviving a small X, the same card would be a wipe, a rebuild and a drain in one. That is a claim that must be resolved before it is printed.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Grave Pact under the verified engine: seven activations is seven edicts, but how many creatures actually die?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Every engine stack on this deck measured the DRAIN and none measured the board. Grave Pact reads 'Whenever a creature you control dies, each other player sacrifices a creature of their choice', and stacks 002/003/005/008 established chains of five to thirteen activations, each of which kills at least one creature you control — and on the Nest lines often two (the sacrificed body and the counter-killed token). If both deaths count, a chain the drain ledger scores at 7 opposing life is simultaneously fourteen edicts per seat, which is a board wipe that leaves your side intact. The Nest-token half is the crux: a token dies to state-based actions for 0 toughness, and stack 003 (pass) already established that this IS a 'dies' event under CR 704.5f / 704.5d / 700.4 for drain purposes. Whether it is also a Grave Pact trigger follows on the same reading but has not been resolved on this board, and the choice-of-sacrifice clause means what opponents actually lose is a separate count from the trigger count.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Nim Deathmantle + Ashnod's Altar: which body makes the loop pay for itself, and what does it produce here?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: bracket_report.json lists Nim Deathmantle + Ashnod's Altar as a contained two-card infinite, and combo_details also records the three-card forms with Grave Titan (popularity 2,013) and Woe Strider (1,546). The arithmetic is not obviously self-funding on the two-card reading: Ashnod's Altar adds {2} per sacrifice and the Deathmantle trigger costs {4}, so a single nontoken body returns at a two-sacrifice rate and needs a second body per cycle — which is exactly what Grave Titan (two 2/2 Zombie tokens on enter) or Woe Strider (a 0/1 Goat) supplies. Worth resolving because the payoff in THIS deck is not the mana: the Deathmantle makes its equipped creature a black Zombie, which switches Gravecrawler on and, with Ayara out, is a black creature entering every cycle. A scenario should state which body it assumes and count the creation-side triggers, not just the mana.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Gravecrawler + Phyrexian Altar: the two-card tag hides a board condition
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The most popular contained line in the deck (combo_details popularity 60,592) and tagged a two-card infinite in bracket_report.json — but Gravecrawler's own text conditions the recursion, 'You may cast this card from your graveyard as long as you control a Zombie', and Gravecrawler cannot be that Zombie while it is in the graveyard. So the line as contained needs a third permanent that is a Zombie (Warren Soultrader, Gray Merchant of Asphodel, Mikaeus, a Grave Titan token, or a Nim Deathmantle-equipped creature). Phyrexian Altar's {B} exactly pays the recast, so the loop is mana-neutral and produces unbounded death and ETB triggers — drainless on its own, and lethal only with a payoff attached, which is the same shape stack 001 (pass) proved for the Blowfly loop: 'genuinely unbounded' but 'drainless here', total drain 'exactly 3 per opponent'. The parallel is close enough that the scenario should be written to test it rather than to assume the happier reading.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: You are the CONTROL here too, and that is the uncomfortable part — two decks both claiming inevitability means the one with the cheaper rebuild wins, and yours is cheaper. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math: 'After the wrath, initiative goes to whoever rebuilds cheapest: redeploy worst-first, keeping the best threat in hand for their second sweeper', with the Commander correction that you should 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package'. This deck's rebuild package is structural rather than held: Reassembling Skeleton returns for {1}{B} forever, Gravecrawler recasts for {B} while a Zombie is out, Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections make a body a turn without spending a card, and Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Phyrexian Reclamation buy back whatever ate the removal. Plumb the Forbidden converts the wrath itself into cards at instant speed. The one line to refuse is the all-in board: the same section's rule is to 'commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further', and the drain rates make 'what wins' countable — 7 per opponent with a death-metering drain, 13 with Mirkwood Bats (stacks 003 and 008, both pass). Deploy the outlet and the fodder; hold the drain until the turn it converts.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: The commander's ability costs no mana, which is the best single property a deck can have under a tax — and the doc reaches this without naming it. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial says 'Decks built on many cheap spells per turn are hit hardest: taxes attack the velocity math directly, so recount your hand under the tax', but 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature' is paid in life and bodies, so a Sphere effect does not touch it once Yawgmoth has resolved. Deployment is the vulnerable window, not operation. That inverts the section's usual role assignment: it says 'you rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown, racing the lock's completion', and here you often DO own it, because the lock has to answer a resource it does not tax. Two exposures remain — fast mana is thin (3 cards, 43.5% unassisted / 78.2% assisted by turn 10) so a tax landing before turn four genuinely delays a commander whose mean cast turn is 4.283; and the interaction suite is 3 dedicated instants plus 4 sweepers, short of the section's requirement that 'some answers must be castable under the tax'. Name the out early — the piece that stops YOU, not the scariest piece (strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs).
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: You are the aggressor's target and the pod's stabiliser, and this deck is unusually good at both jobs at once. strategy:card-advantage.virtual is the frame: 'a card that blanks several opposing cards generates advantage without drawing anything', with the Commander correction that 'virtual advantage triples — one tax or pillow-fort effect can blank attack plans from three players at once'. Grave Pact is that card here: every creature you sacrifice edicts every other player, so an aggressive board is dismantled by an engine you were running anyway. Four sweepers (Toxic Deluge, Black Sun's Zenith, Carnifex Demon, Soul Snuffers) plus nine debuff effects mean the deck answers boards rather than threats — which matters, because strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy sets the bar for spot removal at 'ends the game or ends my deck's function', and with three dedicated instants you cannot spend one on the biggest creature. Life is what you are feeding the engine (1 per Yawgmoth activation, 1 per Soultrader activation, plus Necropotence and Bitterblossom), so strategy:life-as-resource's discipline binds hard: know 'when your life total has become real... and switching from spending to defending one turn before it matters, not one after'. The drains cut both ways — 13 per opponent from one Bats assembly is 13 you did not have to race for.
matchup_frames.vs_combo: The unfavourable matchup, and the honest reading is that you are the beatdown against it while remaining the control against everyone else at the same table — strategy:whos-the-beatdown's Commander correction is explicit: 'you can be the beatdown against one opponent and the control against another in the same turn cycle; assign per-threat, not per-game'. Your interaction against a combo turn is three instants (Deadly Rollick, Fatal Push, Snuff Out), two of which answer only creatures; there are no counterspells. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite's breadth rule — 'three opponents mean every permanent type appears, so cover the classes — creature, artifact, enchantment, graveyard, land — before doubling any' — is not met, and this is where the deck pays for its engine. What you have instead is speed with a floor: strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy's countervailing clause applies, 'against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now', so hold nothing. Bojuka Bog is a free graveyard answer riding on a land drop. The plan is to be the faster clock: the engine's four enabler classes sit at 73–74% unassisted and about 90% assisted by turn 10, and one Bats assembly is 52 of the pod's 160 life — pace for that, not for the tutored kill.
matchup_frames.vs_graveyard_hate: Worth its own line, because the deck's renewable-fodder QUALITY is graveyard-resident: Gravecrawler recasts from the graveyard, Reassembling Skeleton returns from it, and Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Phyrexian Reclamation all read from it. A Rest in Peace effect does not stop the engine — Nest of Scarabs, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, Sedgemoor Witch and Grave Titan make bodies without it, and Yawgmoth's ability never touches the graveyard — but it converts renewable fodder back into one-shot fodder, which is precisely the axis the deck buys its consistency on. strategy:threat-assessment ranks by 'interaction cost (what answering it later costs versus now)': graveyard hate is cheap to answer on the way in and expensive afterwards, so this is one of the few cases where spending a dedicated instant on a non-creature permanent is correct even though the spot removal is thin.

distribution_notes: Deck-facts reports 79 entries across 100 copies (the 99 plus the commander), 64 nonland cards, and 36 land COPIES across 15 land entries — 22 of them Swamp, which is why entries and copies must never be confused. Curve: 14 at one mana, 15 at two, 19 at three, 11 at four, 2 at five, 3 at six. Against strategy:deckbuilding.curve's EDHREC baseline (modal mana value 2, '15.7 two-drops and 15.4 three-drops in the average deck and only ~1.5 cards at mana value 8+'), this list is a hair heavier at three and dramatically lighter at the top — five cards above four mana in the entire 99 — which is the right shape for a deck the same section describes as buying 'cheap enablers'. Mana: 35 black land sources against the 36 a 90% on-curve rate would take, lifted to 43 by rocks and dorks, on-curve probability 0.895 lands-only and 0.960 with rocks (mana_analysis.json); 75 black pips across 54 cards, max 3; four lands enter tapped; deck-facts reports NO restricted mana anywhere in the deck. The 36-land count lands exactly on Nate Burgess's starting point as relayed in strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base — 'lands = 31 + colours in the commander's identity + the commander's mana value' — 31 + 1 + 4 = 36. Roles (card_roles.json, 97.5% coverage): 9 sac outlets, 12 sac costs, 9 drains, 5 recursion, 5 unrestricted tutors, 10 ramp pieces across dork/ritual/rock plus 4 treasure makers, 3 draw engines and 3 draw bursts. Interaction is where the linear tax shows: 3 dedicated spot-removal instants, 4 sweepers, 1 edict and 9 debuff effects. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite's baseline is 'at least 8-10 removal spells' inside a '15- to 20-card interactive suite' with wipes 'one or two max' (Zupke caps at 3) — this deck inverts it, running MORE wipes than the cap and a third of the spot removal, which strategy:critical-mass explains rather than excuses: 'interaction slots are the price of the engine, so the deck's defense is speed, redundancy, and resilience, not answers'. Two honest costs sit in the numbers. Fast mana is 3 cards at 43.5% unassisted / 78.2% assisted by turn 10, thin for a deck whose best draw is a turn-2 commander; strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors gives the arithmetic that makes it unsurprising — '5 copies is 31% of openers, 7 is 41%... 90% by ten cards seen costs about 20 copies'. And renewable fodder sits at 73.6% unassisted while its per-copy quality is higher than the count suggests: Reassembling Skeleton returns for {1}{B} with no condition and Gravecrawler recasts for {B} while you control a Zombie — and Warren Soultrader, Gray Merchant of Asphodel and Mikaeus are all Zombies, with Grave Titan and Nim Deathmantle making more. The doc has no vocabulary for that distinction: it counts copies of an effect class, not whether a copy comes back. Two cards carry no role pattern at all (Plumb the Forbidden, Supernatural Stamina); deck-facts is explicit that this is a taxonomy hole, not a functional one. Finally, the synergy graph is close to useless here and says so: 39 edges fall inside the deck, seven deck cards including Nest of Scarabs and Exquisite Blood have no entry at all, and deck-facts warns it 'is a top-10 shortlist selected over every tagged card in the format... it cannot tell you how well a card fits this list.'
overall_assessment: This is a control deck that happens to own eleven infinite-combo lines, and every measured number says the engine is the plan while the kills are the ceiling. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math states the discipline the whole issue should be built on: 'Separate ceiling from median: the full storm kill is the ceiling; the median game is the value engine under it — pace for the median, hold the ceiling as opportunism.' The median is exceptionally well supplied — by turn 10 the enabler classes assemble at 73.6% fodder, 73.8% a free sac outlet, 73.0% an ignition source and 66.9% a drain unassisted, rising to roughly 90% with a tutor, and the commander is on the battlefield by turn 6 in 91.7% of games at a mean cast turn of 4.283. The ceiling is real but conditional, and it is FOUR ceilings rather than one — goldfish_metrics.json measures each named kill separately, unassisted / tutor-assisted by turn 10: Blowfly + Nest 2.6% / 32.1%, the Mikaeus package 1.7% / 26.2%, Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar 2.9% / 32.5%, Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler + any drain 1.1% / 20.0%. NO SINGLE ONE OF THOSE NUMBERS CHARACTERISES THE DECK, and nothing in the artifacts does either. The four lines are independent and not mutually exclusive, so the honest quantity — 'can I kill from here' — is their UNION, which is materially larger than the largest of them and is not reported anywhere: the goldfish target schema is an AND of ORs and cannot express a union, so no artifact computes one and none should be invented. The sheet's one composite, 'EITHER kill' at 5.5% / 32.8%, is not that union either; its need block is Nest-or-Mikaeus AND Blowfly-or-Carnifex AND a drain, so it spans two of the four lines and must never be quoted as the deck's kill rate. State it plainly instead: four independent kills exist, each individually reachable in a fifth to a third of games once a tutor is drawn, and the probability that at least one is live is unmeasured and strictly greater than 32.5%. That is exactly what 'the kill is modular rather than singular' means in numbers. The gap between the unassisted and assisted columns is the deck's whole personality, and the right reading is not 'tutor-dependent' — it is that the ENGINE is not tutor-dependent at all and the NAMED kills are, which is a different sentence with different play consequences. What makes this engine unusual is that its conversion rate is measured rather than assumed, and the measurement produced the most instructive result on the deck. On the Yawgmoth line, Mirkwood Bats yields 13 triggers, 13 life from each opponent, 52 across the four-opponent pod (stack 008, checker.verdict == pass; 13 proven a ceiling five separate ways, and the final solve varied only Bats' toughness to give 8 / 10 / 13 / 15 triggers at 0/1/2/3 counter slots). On the Blowfly line, the same card produces 2 and HALTS the loop, because its 2/3 body survives the forced -1/-1 counter, nothing dies, and the unbounded engine simply stops (stack 007, pass). Same card, same body, opposite verdicts — surviving the forced counter is fatal to a loop that needs something to die, and free value on a line that sacrifices deliberately. That is a deckbuilding principle, not a card evaluation, and it is a finding rather than an argument. The structural consequence is the shift from death-metered payoffs to CREATION-metered ones. Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar all meter deaths, and the verified ledger for that class is unflattering: 7 drains and 28 pod life on the engine line (stacks 002 and 003, both pass, 7 proven a ceiling), 8 life total for a single-target drain — a 3.5x penalty against the each-opponent class (stack 004, pass, which refutes Blood Artist as a kill outright), and a CR 119.9 edge on the Avatar line where an Insect killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0, gains 0, and gaining 0 is not a life gain event (stack 005, pass, which also refutes Spellbook's 'Near-infinite' tag for that board). Mirkwood Bats and Ayara, First of Locthwain pay on creation instead — Ayara because 'another black creature you control enters' catches Nest of Scarabs' black Insect tokens — and that is the axis on which conversion actually scales. strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry is the school: prefer 'effects that tax or drain every opponent at once', because 'Your cards should do something to all three seats or win the game'. Grave Pact belongs to the same reading from the other side, converting the identical activations into table-wide edicts. Where this build gains over a single-combo one is layering, and strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density has the exact language: cEDH 'compresses that, its finishers being combos: Eisenherz's rule is two primary combos, a Plan A and Plan B, never more than two *unconnected* ones... Layering reconciles them: overlap pieces, so five cards support four combos'. Forty-two contained lines over roughly twenty pieces is layering at its limit — outlets, fodder and drains are shared across every family, so a removal spell that answers one kill rarely answers only one. The cost is stated in the same section and should not be hidden: 'the ceiling build runs one spectacular finisher and loses when it's answered; the median runs three cheap ones and closes from any board' — this is the median build, so it must actually be piloted as one. Two costs are real and belong in print rather than buried. Fast mana is 3 cards, 43.5% unassisted, in a deck that would love a turn-2 commander and gets a turn-4 one. And renewable fodder counts 73.6% while its quality is high — Reassembling Skeleton unconditional, Gravecrawler nearly so in a shell holding four Zombie sources — a trade the strategy doc has no framework to price, because it counts copies rather than asking whether a copy returns. The bracket floor is 4, forced by four Game Changers and by eleven two-card infinites all assembling at mana value <= 6 (bracket_report.json), with Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar the highest-bracket line present. strategy:deckbuilding.power-level is the right posture for that number: 'Contents give a floor, never a verdict', and Bracket 4 is 'lethal, consistent, and fast', at least four turns. The caveat belongs beside it: seven of those eleven are the Mikaeus family, none is verified, and on plain oracle reading undying leaves a +1/+1 counter that a second sacrifice would find — so whether they are two-card lines or three-card lines routing through the commander's -1/-1 counter is the deck's biggest open question. deck-facts is unambiguous about what that means: 'a line is fact only once a stack artifact carries checker.verdict == pass.' Play it as the deck the numbers describe. Deploy the outlet and the fodder early, keep the drain in hand until the turn it converts, use Yawgmoth as a draw engine for three or four turns before you use him as a kill, count bodies before you go, and go at the seat you can actually kill — strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window's standard is the table's, applied to you: 'does this card win the game if it resolves', and for one assembly the answer is 'against one opponent, yes'.
gaps: No aristocrats / sacrifice-loop section anywhere in the doc. The heading list has nothing on the outlet / fodder / payoff triad, which is this deck's entire architecture, and queries for it top out around 0.23 against Engine-Deck Keeps and Budget. This is the largest hole a research pass could fill and it generalises to every Blood Artist, token-sacrifice and Aristocrats deck in the format.

Nothing on what BOUNDS an iterative engine. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math covers velocity and the go decision but never asks which resource runs out first — bodies, mana, life or library. Every engine stack on this deck ended by body exhaustion, and the deck's whole improvement axis is renewability; the doc has no vocabulary for either.

No theory of trigger SURFACE — creation-side versus death-side payoffs. Stacks 007 and 008 measured the same card at 2 triggers and 13 triggers on two lines in the same deck, the deciding property being whether the payoff's own body survives a forced shrink. The doc has no section in which 'a bigger body is a liability' is even expressible.

strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors counts copies of an effect class and has no notion that a RECURSIVE copy is worth more than a one-shot one. Reassembling Skeleton and Gravecrawler are each one card and unbounded uses; the hypergeometric frame prices them identically to a body that dies once. Renewability belongs in that section's arithmetic.

Nothing on mana-free activated abilities as a class. Yawgmoth's ability costs life and a body, which changes his behaviour under Sphere effects, under Winter Orb, and at instant speed on opponents' end steps. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial and strategy:tempo.sequencing both come close and neither names it — and it is the strongest property this deck has against stax.

No section on life as ENGINE FUEL rather than as a buffer. strategy:life-as-resource treats life as currency spent on cards and turns; this deck spends it per activation on two outlets, on Necropotence, on Bitterblossom and on a commander whose every use costs 1, while gaining it back from drains at a rate that depends on which payoff is out. The break-even reasoning has no home in the doc.

Nothing on how a bracket floor should be discussed when the lines forcing it are unverified. bracket_report.json's own note calls brackets 'a conversation, not a calculator', but the power-level sections give no guidance on the Rule 0 conversation you should have when seven of your eleven infinites are containment records rather than resolved lines.

No theory of what a KILL RATE is when a deck has several kills. The goldfish target schema is an AND of ORs, so it can measure each of this deck's four named kills separately (32.1% / 26.2% / 32.5% / 20.0% tutor-assisted by turn 10) but cannot express the union that actually answers 'can I kill from here' — and its one composite target spans two of the four, so quoting it as the deck's kill rate is wrong twice over. The doc has nothing on reading several partially-overlapping win conditions as one probability, nor on the honest alternative: naming the count of independent lines and declining to fabricate the number. strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density asks you to 'count how many of the 99 produce it' and stops there; strategy:combat-math.probability supplies Karsten's hypergeometric method for one target class at a time. Neither covers overlapping targets, which is the situation every layered combo deck is actually in.
